profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting in an ML research lab between a faculty lead and a senior PhD student who are planning a workshop paper follow-up on guided evolutionary NAS. They have both read the G-EA paper and want to generate ideas for a new variant that can be tested quickly in NAS-Bench-201 and pitched as a more general search strategy for low-compute settings. The immediate context is that the lab has a two-week window before an internal deadline for selecting one project to push into experiments. The agenda is to brainstorm 2-3 promising extensions to guided evolutionary NAS, decide what kind of lightweight validation would make an idea worth prototyping, and sketch what the first experiment package should include. The expected outcome is a shortlist of candidate directions and a shared sense that they can start a small pilot immediately, even though some second-order assumptions remain quietly misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Mira Shen
members.expertise: Neural architecture search, efficient model selection, empirical ML methodology
members.background: Leads a university ML systems and AutoML lab; previously published on zero-cost proxies and benchmark-driven NAS evaluation; often frames brainstorming around publishable conceptual contributions and compact experimental packages.
members.private_state: She wants a workshop-paper-worthy angle that can be demonstrated quickly without committing major compute, and she is especially concerned that the idea look methodologically clean and transferable beyond one benchmark.
hidden_assumptions: When discussing a 'pilot' for NAS ideas, the search itself should run in the tabular benchmark first, with any real training limited to a very small confirmation stage afterward.

A 'general' NAS contribution can be argued from showing the mechanism behaves consistently across the three standard NAS-Bench-201 datasets, even if all evidence comes from that single benchmark family.
When someone says an approach is 'lightweight', that refers primarily to not increasing the number of fully trained candidate architectures during search.
If they agree to keep the method 'close to G-EA', the default execution is to preserve the one-survivor-per-generation dynamic and only modify guidance signals around it.

members.name: Leo Park
members.expertise: Evolutionary search, reproducible training pipelines, proxy-based evaluation
members.background: Fourth-year PhD student who maintains the lab's NAS codebase and has recently been adapting benchmark ideas to small real-training pipelines on CIFAR and Tiny-ImageNet; he tends to translate brainstorming into implementable experiment flows.
members.private_state: He wants an idea that can become a substantial thesis chapter, ideally something that survives outside the benchmark tables, and he is concerned about investing in a method that only looks good because of benchmark conveniences.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' for NAS is only meaningful if the search loop is exercised with actual short training runs on sampled models, because benchmark lookup alone can hide implementation artifacts.
Calling a method 'general' implies at least one result outside NAS-Bench-201-style tabular replay, even if the main experiments stay small.
When someone says an approach is 'lightweight', that refers to wall-clock practicality of the whole pipeline, including zero-proxy computation, mutation bookkeeping, and short-list retraining.
If they agree to stay 'close to G-EA', the core idea is guided selection plus age-aware exploration, but the survivor structure can be relaxed as long as the search remains recognizably evolutionary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with a 'small pilot' before committing to full experiments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the pilot means running the search loop by querying NAS-Bench-201 results and only doing a tiny real-training sanity check on the final shortlisted architecture or two.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the pilot means implementing the search loop over actually instantiated networks with short-budget training during search, even if only on CIFAR-10 and with few generations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In NAS meetings, 'pilot' naturally signals a low-commitment first pass, and both see themselves as proposing a lightweight validation step, so neither feels a need to unpack the exact execution mode.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the new idea should 'generalize' or be 'more general than G-EA.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the mechanism should produce stable gains across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120 within NAS-Bench-201, indicating robustness across tasks in the benchmark.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the method should plausibly transfer beyond tabular NAS-Bench-201, ideally to at least one non-tabular or partially trained search setting, even if with modest evidence.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use 'generalization' in a positive, research-standard way; because benchmarking across multiple datasets often stands in for broader robustness, the stronger external-validity interpretation remains implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of staying close to G-EA
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to keep the first variant 'close to G-EA.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes preserving the original population logic—evaluate many at initialization, train only the top architecture, and carry a single winner forward each generation—while only modifying ranking or age bias.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this only requires preserving guided evolutionary search with age/exploration pressure; he is comfortable expanding to a small survivor set or archive if it makes the method more stable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are discussing incremental follow-ups rather than radical redesigns, 'close to G-EA' feels self-explanatory and neither expects the other to interpret the phrase at the level of population-state boundaries.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They want the idea to remain 'lightweight' or 'without extra compute.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means not increasing the number of fully trained architectures relative to G-EA; extra proxy calculations or bookkeeping are acceptable if training cost stays flat.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the end-to-end runtime and engineering overhead should stay small; a method that avoids full training but adds heavy proxy ensembles or repeated rescoring is no longer lightweight.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In efficient NAS, training cost is the headline bottleneck, so M1's interpretation sounds standard, while M2 silently folds in implementation/runtime concerns from practice; both can sincerely endorse 'lightweight' without noticing the mismatch.

turns.inner_thought: We only have two weeks to decide whether this is workshop-material, so I need something that can be demonstrated fast and cleanly. A small pilot should mean replaying the search in NAS-Bench-201, checking whether the mechanism looks consistent, and then maybe training one or two final picks just to avoid the obvious criticism that it's purely table-driven. If the effect is tidy across the three datasets, that's already enough to motivate a compact follow-up.
turns.utterance: Given the two-week window, I think we should frame this as a small pilot around guided evolutionary NAS and only push further if we find a really clean angle.

turns.inner_thought: That makes sense, as long as the pilot actually exercises the search loop in code and not just benchmark replay. What I like about G-EA is that the guidance at initialization gives it a distinct identity, so if we stay close to G-EA but make it less brittle, I can probably wire something into the existing pipeline quickly and learn whether it survives real short-budget runs.
turns.utterance: Yeah, the nice part of G-EA for me is that initialization-stage guidance already gives us a handle, so maybe we brainstorm variants that stay close to G-EA but smooth out some of the brittleness.

turns.inner_thought: An easy paper angle would be uncertainty or confidence on top of the proxy, without changing the core one-winner-per-generation structure. That keeps it close to G-EA in the way I care about: same population logic, just a better guidance signal. As long as we are not increasing the number of fully trained architectures, it's still lightweight, even if we do some extra proxy-side computation.
turns.utterance: One straightforward direction is to make the proxy score confidence-aware, so the method stays lightweight and we still only train the most convincing candidate each generation.

turns.inner_thought: A confidence signal is nice, but if the search keeps collapsing onto one path too early, I may want a tiny archive to stabilize it. I still think that counts as close to G-EA because the search remains guided and evolutionary; relaxing the survivor structure a bit is not a conceptual departure. And for the pilot, I really want to see whether this behaves more stably when the actual search loop runs with short training, not just in a lookup replay.
turns.utterance: I could see that, and maybe a tiny survivor archive goes well with it, so the pilot can tell us whether guided evolution is just a bit more stable in practice.

turns.inner_thought: An archive is acceptable if it doesn't bloat the story or muddy the comparison. What I need is a general argument, and for me that means the same mechanism should show a consistent pattern across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120 within NAS-Bench-201. If it only helps on one dataset, the angle becomes too narrow for a neat workshop package.
turns.utterance: An archive could be interesting if it still feels general and we see the same pattern across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120.

turns.inner_thought: Right, but I don't want us to call something general if it only works in tabular replay. At minimum I'd like one result where the search loop isn't just benchmark lookup, even if it's small and messy compared with the benchmark side. Otherwise I worry we'll end up with another method that looks great because the table hides implementation issues.
turns.utterance: I agree. For it to really feel general, I'd want the idea to survive at least one setting where the search loop isn't just benchmark lookup, even if the main story stays small.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as a sanity layer later, but the main thing now is a mechanism we can test quickly. Another clean option is age-adjusted rescoring every few generations while preserving the G-EA backbone as I understand it. That should still be without extra compute in the important sense, because we wouldn't be training additional architectures beyond the usual path.
turns.utterance: Another variant might be age-adjusted rescoring every few generations. That still seems close to G-EA, and it should remain without extra compute if we're not training more architectures.

turns.inner_thought: Rescoring is plausible, but only if the runtime doesn't quietly balloon from repeated proxy passes and extra state tracking. To me lightweight has to include the full loop, not just the number of trained models. And if we do keep some survivors around, it needs to stay very small or I'll lose half the week in engineering details.
turns.utterance: Rescoring could work, yeah, as long as the lightweight version doesn't blow up runtime and the survivor set stays small enough that I can implement it quickly.

turns.inner_thought: We should keep the first package minimal: baseline G-EA versus one modified variant, run through the benchmark family, then a brief real-training sanity check at the end on the shortlisted result. That's enough for an early go/no-go and keeps the narrative methodologically clean.
turns.utterance: For the pilot package, I'd keep it simple: vanilla G-EA against one modified variant, and then a brief sanity-check training run after the search.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, I'll hook the modified search into the training pipeline itself and keep the generations short so we get an early signal. If it works there, I can still mirror part of it in the benchmark setup afterward. He's probably mostly thinking about a minimal package, which is fine, but I need the pilot to expose real implementation behavior from the start.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. I can set up the pilot by wiring the modified search into the existing training pipeline and keeping the generations small so we get an early read.

turns.inner_thought: Good. The main thing is that we pick something incremental enough to execute quickly and present clearly: a close-to-G-EA variant, probably age-aware guidance around the existing structure, lightweight in terms of training cost, and ideally general in the sense of consistent behavior across the standard datasets. If that lands, it's exactly the sort of compact contribution I want.
turns.utterance: So the front-runner seems to be a close-to-G-EA variant with some age-aware guidance that stays lightweight and ideally looks general.

turns.inner_thought: That's enough to get moving. I'll draft a pilot plan around the most implementable version first, probably the one that gives us the best chance of holding up outside the neat benchmark case, and then we can decide how much evidence we need once the first runs come back.
